title: 3-D: candidate A complete; fourth candidate D added
tldr: Candidate A (13.5 mm throat, 22 mm outlet, port +9 mm) with the long-radius reducer, 6–100 L/min, 3-D, agent-checked: dose varies 1.73× over 6–100 L/min; the head fills at 28.9 L/min and overflows at 31.3, above the handpump range. In 3-D the elbow lowers throat suction ~10% vs 2-D, which leaves the 6 L/min end high; the port alone cannot rebalance it. Candidate D (same throat and outlet, V1 port position) added to the 3-D queue because it should balance better in 3-D.
body: p
Plot: home/cand_3d.png (B, C, D appear as they finish).
list
V1 (same setup, 6–30 L/min): 1.82×. Current part: 1.30× over 6–30, but 1.51× by 60 L/min and still climbing steeply; it overflows the Afridev at 18.5 L/min.

Why A is 1.73× in 3-D vs 1.63× in 2-D: the elbow's inflow profile cuts throat suction by ~10% (3-D/2-D 0.90 at 20–45 L/min), which raises the relative weight of the 6 L/min water column. A 3-D virtual port scan along A's wall shows ports anywhere in the throat give 1.67–1.73×; moving into the diffuser is worse. So the fix is the shape's balance, not the port.

Rule from this: shapes slightly under-tuned in 2-D (2-D s0/k ≈ 150–160) should balance best in 3-D. C (161) is already queued; D = R2_0_t13.5_n22 (154) added. A vs D isolates the port position, C vs D the outlet size.

Agent check of A's sweep: all 8 flows converged (first 1" runs above 60 L/min). Caveat: at 70–100 L/min the wall y+ rises to 13–19 (mean), so high-flow suction may be slightly under-predicted; this does not change the spread, which the 6 L/min end sets.
Long-radius vs E-Sig + elbow (earlier V1–V4 runs): piped consistency is the same within ~3%; the long-radius elbow's lower loss delays handpump overflow by ~5–7 L/min.
p
Queue: long-radius B, C, D (done ~10 pm), then E-Sig + elbow for all four (~8 am Fri), then the outlet-vane test (~9:30 am Fri).

title: CAD drafts of A, B, C and the first 3-D results for A
tldr: Threaded CAD drafts of the three candidates are in the CAD tab (STEP + 3-D preview). Same thread, stop collar, injector port (1/4-28 for the existing ferrule, nut and PTFE tube), lettering and outlet vanes as the rev3 V1; only the bore changes. Water path probed end to end on the exported files: open everywhere except where the outlet vanes cross the axis, exactly as on V1. 3-D of A so far (long-radius reducer): more suction than V1 at every flow and the head fills only near 30 L/min.
body: list

Checks on each part: single valid solid, injector orifice open, no clash with the injector fitting, 1.65 mm wall under the thread (as V1), water path open on the axis and at 85% of the bore radius every 0.5 mm, wall solid behind the bore, outlet ~85–88% open (vanes).

3-D, candidate A + long-radius reducer (V1 in brackets): 6 L/min suction 1.15 kPa (1.05), 10 L/min 1.45 (1.29), 20 L/min 2.84 (2.41), 30 L/min 5.31 (4.38). Water level at 30 L/min +3.5 cm (+2.8): head fills just below 30 L/min, overflow ~32, above the handpump range.

Trade-off now visible in 3-D: over 6–30 L/min A varies 1.73× (V1 1.82×, current part 1.30×). A design tuned for 6–100 L/min gives a higher dose at 6–10 L/min than at 20; the current part is flatter at low flow but climbs steeply above 40 L/min and overflows the handpump at 18.5 L/min. Question to the team: which piped flow range matters most?
Open question: keep V1's outlet vanes on the new parts? With 20–22 mm outlets they block ~13–15% of the outlet and are not in the CFD.

title: Round 2 complete; three candidates picked and in 3-D
tldr: Round 2 (14 shapes, 84 cases) finished and passed an independent check. Across both rounds (32 shapes, 210 cases) the best piped shapes are a 13.5–14 mm throat with a 20–22 mm outlet nozzle, at 1.63–1.66× over 6–100 L/min against a 1.62× limit for any fixed bore. Three candidates (A, B, C) went straight into 3-D with both reducers; results this evening (long-radius) and early Friday (E-Sig + elbow).
body: p
Plot, bore profiles and top-12 table: home/r2_candidates.png.
list
A: 13.5 mm throat, 22 mm outlet, port 9 mm higher (30° inlet cone). 1.63×; suction at 6 L/min 1.19 kPa (highest of the three).
B: 14 mm throat, 22 mm outlet, port 10 mm lower (24 mm throat). 1.66×; the widest throat, so the pump head should fill latest on the handpump; suction at 6 L/min 0.97 kPa.
C: 13.5 mm throat, 20 mm outlet, round 1 port. 1.64×; the 20 mm outlet gives the most margin for running full at 6 L/min.
All three keep the outlet running full at 6 L/min (exit speed ≥ 1.6× the air-bubble rise speed).
p
Honest read:
list

The top dozen shapes all sit within 1.63–1.69×; their dose curves nearly coincide. On piped consistency alone the candidates beat V1 (1.67×) by only 2–3%. The real differences are the outlet staying full at 6 L/min (V1's 26 mm outlet does not), the suction margin at 6 L/min, and handpump overflow.
Feed-law sensitivity (shown in the table): if the true exponent were 0.6 the spread would be ~1.9×, if 1.0 ~3.6× for these throats. The pipe-rig test will check the exponent.

Against the current part: its 3-D curve is flatter from 6 to 60 L/min (1.51×) but it rises steeply above 40 L/min (≈1.96× extrapolated to 100) and overflows the Afridev at 18.5 L/min. The 3-D runs put the candidates on the same footing.
p

Round 2 check (agent): all 84 cases clean, meshes OK (30° cone non-orthogonality 30°, fillet R14 verified), residuals ≤ 3e-6, wall matches the design stations exactly, no flow separation at the port in the steeper-cone shapes, the port shift changed the 6 L/min suction by the expected ±0.1 kPa, spreads recomputed by hand.
p

3-D plan: the long-radius reducer at 6–100 L/min for A, B, C first (~12 h), then the E-Sig + 1" elbow at 6–70 L/min (~7 h); one 8-core case at a time. Each new mesh is agent-checked. Then: handpump model on the 3-D curves, CAD drafts.

title: Round 1 complete: the flat-dose optimum is a broad 13.5–14 mm zone
tldr: All 126 round 1 cases finished and passed two independent checks. With the outlet sized to run full at 6 L/min, the 13.5 mm throat + 20 mm outlet is best at 1.64× over 6–100 L/min, against 1.62× for the best possible fixed bore. 13 mm/20 is 1.70×, 14 mm/20 1.76×; with a 23 mm outlet 13.5 and 14 mm are 1.67–1.69×. Round 2 (port position, 22 mm outlet) runs through the morning, then the 3 candidates go to 3-D.
body: p
Plot and full table: home/r1_full.png.
list
With 23 mm outlets (outlet only marginally full at 6 L/min): 13.5/23 1.67×, 14/23 1.69×. Round 2's 22 mm outlet sits between.
Over 6–120 L/min, 14/23 (1.75×) and 14/20 (1.76×) edge ahead of 13.5/20 (1.78×): narrower throats lose a little at the top end.
Trade-off: narrower throats lose more head, so the handpump head fills and overflows sooner (rough 2-D estimate: 13.5 mm ~28 L/min, 14 mm ~28–31). The 3-D runs will settle this.
Suction at 6 L/min: 1.06–1.15 kPa for every shape; the current part has 0.89 kPa (3-D).
p

Independent check of the 12.5–13.5 mm cases: all 63 complete and clean (mesh OK, non-orthogonality 20°, y+ ≤ 2.3, residuals ≤ 2e-6, mass balance ≤ 2e-7). No case was run twice by the two drivers. Spread recomputed by hand. One note: with the free 26 mm outlet the narrow throats show a little backflow at the outlet at 6–10 L/min, another reason to use the 20–22 mm outlet nozzle.

title: Round 1, 14–16 mm throats complete: 14 mm is the flattest, within 4% of the best possible
tldr: All 63 cases (14/15/16 mm throats × 26/23/20 mm outlets × 6–120 L/min) finished clean and passed an independent check. The 14 mm throat (V1's) gives the flattest piped dose: 1.67× (26 mm outlet), 1.69× (23 mm), 1.76× (20 mm) over 6–100 L/min, against 1.62× for the best any fixed bore can do. 15 mm is 1.86–2.02×, 16 mm 2.05–2.49×. The 12.5–13.5 mm throats and round 2 finish overnight.
body: p
Plot: r1_t14_16.png on this site (home/r1_t14_16.png).
list

Every shape's dose is highest at 6 L/min and lowest near 20–40 L/min; for 14 mm the 6 L/min and 100 L/min ends are about equal, which is what a balanced (near-optimal) bore looks like. Wider throats are dominated by the 6 L/min end.
The smaller outlets cost a little consistency (14 mm: 1.67 → 1.76× going from 26 to 20 mm) but are needed to keep the outlet running full at 6 L/min. Round 2 adds a 22 mm outlet as the compromise.
Suction at 6 L/min is 1.01–1.08 kPa for all nine shapes (current part 0.89 kPa in 3-D), almost all of it the water column below the port.
p

Independent check (agent): all 63 meshes OK (non-orthogonality 20°, y+ max 2.0 at 120 L/min), residuals ≤ 1e-5, mass balance ~1e-8, port pressure not drifting, geometry matches the design stations to 0.000 mm, scoring recomputed by hand. Two scoring-script caveats fixed (shapes with partial flows are now ranked last; the port scan's measured spread now uses 6–100 L/min only).
p

Watch item: at 6 L/min the flow runs backwards along most of the diffuser wall in every shape (low Reynolds number), 6–32% at 10 L/min, and is attached from 20 L/min up. The port, in the throat, is upstream of it, and suction at 6 L/min is still clear; the bench at 6 L/min will tell whether it matters.

title: Round 2 queued; handpump model now matches the V1 bench
tldr: Round 2 (14 shapes: port moved up or down, 20/22 mm outlets) is queued and starts as round 1 frees cores; an independent check passed its geometry and driver. Early round 1 numbers put the flattest piped curve near a 14 mm throat (V1-sized) with a 20–23 mm outlet. The upgraded handpump model reproduces the V1 bench and shows why: the dose is even while the pump head never fills, and doubles (then overflows) once it does.
body: p
Round 1 so far (40 of 126 cases, no failures; 6–40 L/min only, so not final):
list
14 mm throat: water column ÷ throat loss (s0/k) ≈ 190–225, right at the ~180 the feed law calls for. Spread 1.67–1.76× over 6–40 L/min.
15–16 mm: s0/k 260–510, spreads 1.86–2.30×. Too wide, as expected.
20 mm outlet keeps the outlet full at 6 L/min (exit speed 2.05× the bubble rise speed; 26 mm is 1.07×), at a small cost in spread.

Diffuser: flow reverses along most of the wall at 6 L/min (low Reynolds number) and along 6–30% at 10 L/min; attached at 20 L/min and up for the 26 mm outlet, 1–4% reversed near the nozzle for 20/23 mm. Watching this.
p
Round 2 (14 shapes × 6 flows, 6–100 L/min):
list
Port higher (30° inlet cone, +9 mm column) for 12.5, 13, 13.5 mm throats; port lower (24 mm throat, −10 mm) for 13.5 and 14 mm; plus a 22 mm outlet for the round 1 layout.
First in the queue: the 120/100/70 L/min cases for the 12.5–13.5 mm round 1 shapes, so round 1 completes sooner.
Independent agent check: all 14 profiles monotonic, ports inside the straight throat, angles exact, mesher accepts them; driver never touches another driver's case.
p
Handpump model v2 (bore-top priming from the two-phase run + chlorine flow ∝ suction^0.73):
list
V1, long-radius, model vs bench mg/L: 6.9 L/min 0.23 vs 0.31; 13.8 0.96 vs 0.93; 14.1 0.97 vs 0.91; 19.5 1.00 vs 1.32; 26 1.05 vs 1.32. The 3.4 L/min bench point (0.48) is not reproduced.

While the level stays below the inlet-bore top, air reaches the throat each stroke and the dose sits at about half the piped value, but steadily. Once the head fills, the dose doubles and the Afridev overflows within ~2 L/min (current part 16→18.5 L/min, V12 21→23, V1 29.5→32).

Design consequence: for an even handpump dose the head should not fill anywhere in the pump's range (up to ~26 L/min). This favours a low-loss, V1-like throat, which is also where round 1 puts the flattest piped curve.
p
Next: round 1 t14–16 finishes ~21:00 and gets an agent check; round 2 runs overnight; ranking Thursday morning.

Two rounds of 2-D screening finish by Thursday morning, 3-D confirmation runs Thursday to Friday morning, and CAD is drafted in parallel.

Pass criteria for a candidate: piped dose spread ≤ 1.8× over 6–100 L/min with the measured feed law; handpump overflow above 22 L/min (3-D, long-radius reducer); clear suction at 6 L/min with the outlet running full; no diffuser separation above 10 L/min; body ≤ 125 mm.
p

Risks: the elbow's swirl can shift 2-D results (that's why 3-D is in the loop); the 100 L/min end is extrapolated until the 3-D run there; the feed law was fitted on one device type (results also shown for exponents 0.6–0.8).

title: Pipe-flow bench data recalibrates the dose model: aim for a ~13 mm throat
tldr: Your 7 current-part curves on steady pipe flow fit chlorine flow ∝ suction^0.73 to within 5%. With that law the current part is already fairly consistent on piped flow (1.3–1.5× from 6 to 38 L/min); its real problem is handpump overflow. The flattest possible fixed shape spans 6–100 L/min at about 1.6×, with a throat of about 13 mm, so round 1 was redirected from 14–18 mm to 12.5–16 mm.
body: p

How the fit works: the 3-D CFD of the current part gives its port suction at every flow. If chlorine flow goes as suction^n, the dose goes as suction^n ÷ flow. Each device gets its own scale (needle setting), and one n is fitted to all seven curves.
list
Best n = 0.73 (range 0.69–0.77), rms error 5%.
n = 1 (fully viscous needle valve, my earlier assumption): 29% error. n = 0.5 (orifice): 25%.
The model reproduces the measured shape: dose high at 6 L/min (×1.32 vs measured 1.24–1.40), lowest near 15, rising to ×1.23 at 38 (measured 1.16–1.47).
p
What changes:
list
Corrected: the current part's piped spread is 1.3× over 6–38 L/min (1.96× extrapolated to 100), not the 5.8× I posted earlier under n = 1.
Ranking flips: V1 1.83×, V2 2.43×, V3 3.12× over 6–100 L/min. Large throats are now the worst, because the water column below the port over-feeds at low flow.

Best possible fixed Venturi (suction = column + k·Q²): about 1.6× over 6–100 L/min when column ÷ k ≈ 180. In the 1" V-layout that means a throat of about 13–13.5 mm. A 13 mm throat should overflow the handpump only above about 25 L/min (between V12 at 22.9 and V1 above 30).
p

Round 1 redirected without stopping anything: the 17 and 18 mm shapes were dropped, and 12.5, 13 and 13.5 mm throats (each with 26, 23 and 20 mm outlets) were added on the 4 spare cores. Next round will vary the port position, which sets the column, around the column ÷ k ≈ 180 target.

title: Round 1 shape screen running; current part added for comparison
tldr: [Superseded in part by the 16:30 bench-data update: the piped-flow numbers here assumed chlorine flow ∝ suction; the measured law is suction^0.73.] 15 new bore shapes are being simulated at 7 flows from 6 to 120 L/min (105 cases). The first cases are finishing cleanly; the full ranking is due about 10 pm tonight. The existing part is now shown next to every new design on this site.
body: p

Round 1 varies two things: throat diameter (14, 15, 16, 17, 18 mm) and outlet diameter (26 mm as V1–V3, or a short contraction to 23 or 20 mm). Everything else is held at the V1 layout: 1" inlet, 20° inlet cone, 14 mm long throat, port 7 mm down the throat, 4° diffuser, 125 mm body.
p

Why the outlet contraction: at 6 L/min almost all the port suction comes from the water column below the port. That column only exists if the outlet runs full. In a 26 mm outlet at 6 L/min the water moves down about as fast as an air bubble rises, so air can creep in. A 20–23 mm outlet keeps it full, and it also trims suction at high flow, which flattens the dose.
list
Pipeline check: the 2-D setup re-ran V1 at 30 L/min and matched the earlier result to every digit (level 1.833 cm, port −5.116 kPa).
Independent agent audit: all 15 shapes match the intended geometry to 0.005 mm; all meshes pass checkMesh (non-orthogonality 20°, 51–54k cells); wall cells stay fine enough (y+ ≈ 1) up to 120 L/min.
Speed: about 46 min per case with 12 running at once; done about 10 pm.
p

Current part, for reference (3-D, its own 3/4" E-Sig + elbow train): it overflows the Afridev at about 18.5 L/min, and on piped flow its dose varies 3.4× over 6–60 L/min (about 5.8× extrapolated to 100). Every new candidate is measured against it and against V1.

title: New goal: steady piped dosing from 6 to 100+ L/min, bore shape only
tldr: [Superseded in part by the 16:30 bench-data update: the piped-flow numbers here assumed chlorine flow ∝ suction; the measured law is suction^0.73.] The redesign now targets consistent dosing on piped flow from 6 to over 100 L/min, a working dose at 6 L/min, and no handpump overflow, changing only the Venturi bore. Of the existing designs V2 (16 mm) is the most even; the best throat looks like 16.5–17 mm.
body: p

Dose consistency on piped flow depends on how port suction grows with flow. Suction has two parts: the water column below the port (about 1 kPa, independent of flow) and a throat term that grows with flow². The needle valve passes bleach at about 1 mL/min, a viscous flow, so chlorine flow is proportional to suction and dose is proportional to suction ÷ flow.
list
Small throats (V1, 14 mm): the flow² term dominates early, so they overdose at high flow (dose spread 3.3× over 6–100 L/min).
Large throats (V3, 18 mm): the column dominates, so they underdose at low flow (2.5×).
Best balance for 6–100 L/min: column ≈ 600 × throat coefficient, about a 16.5–17 mm throat, spread about 2.2×. That fits the 0.3–0.8 mg/L band at one needle setting (2.67×).
p
Excluded on the user's call: any added part (flap, valve, vent, riser). The vent two-phase run was stopped at 0.33 s.

title: Narrow throats V10–V12 complete: they overflow inside the handpump range
tldr: Five designs at nine flows (6–30 L/min) in 3-D, all converged. Narrower throats give more suction but back the water up: V10 overflows at 14.8 L/min, V11t at 20.5, V12 at 22.9. No fixed throat keeps the Venturi full and below overflow from 10 to 20 L/min on the handpump.
body: p

The handpump window is set by two levels in the pump head: above the inlet bore top (+2.2 cm) the Venturi stays full; above +5.8 cm the Afridev overflows. Level rises with flow², so any fixed shape stays in that window over a flow ratio of only about 1.08×. Shape moves the window; it can't widen it.
p
V1 already doses within the acceptable 0.1–1.5 mg/L on the bench from 7 to 26 L/min, so the new design must not raise the level much above V1's.

title: Two-phase handpump simulation: why dosing drops at low pump rates
tldr: V1 at 80 clicks/min (13.2 L/min): the pump head drains, and once the level falls below the top of the inlet bore, air runs along the bore into the Venturi. Suction is lost for part of every stroke and the dose falls to about half.
body: list
Suction weakens at 2.72 s; the port goes dry at 2.73 s; the outlet stops running full at 2.76 s.
After air reaches the Venturi the solver's time step falls ~10× (bubbly flow).
This explains the bench result: 0.31 mg/L at 6.9 L/min vs 1.32 at 19.5 L/min.

title: CAD rev3: blocked bore in the long-radius elbow fixed
tldr: The elbow sent on Nov 22 had a 3 mm solid wall across the bore at the coupler flange. Rev3 fixes it; every CAD change now gets an end-to-end water-path probe of the exported file before it is sent.
body: p
Reprint only the elbow; V1–V4 were unchanged. Files are in the CAD tab (Threaded set, rev3).
